1 1. Course map, sources, and how to use this manual
This manual is compiled from all files of the Computer Science — programming in C
course (track Foundations of Computer Science, FoCS; fall semester 2026, Tashkent
University of Technology). The course consists of four layers: (1) weekly lectures
— FoCS/TashTech Lectures 4–7 (October 6, 13, 20, and 27, 2026) — review of the
previous topic and a new topic; (2) laboratory exercises based on chapters 5–8 of
the textbook by Ceri, Mandrioli & Sbattella «The Art and Craft of Computing» in
C11-adaptation with CS50 input helpers (getdouble, getchar, getstring); (3) bug hunt
worksheets — ”bug hunting” on conditional constructs and functions, loops, pointers,
and strings; (4) coffee machine project files (week 6 model: Stock, Recipe, Cup).
The manual covers the material of weeks 4–7: data types and operators, control
structures, functions and structures, pointers, strings, and recursion.
Every savol (savollar — questions) from lectures and labs, every test (testlar), ev-
ery atama (atamalar — terms), and every code fragment from slides, labs, and bug
hunts is fully transcribed and provided with a model answer or solution. All code
examples are taken verbatim from the course files; where the PDF extraction listing
was ”broken” with spaces, it has been restored according to the slide’s meaning.
The original instructor formulations are preserved: «Pop quiz», «Prediction», «Exit
check», «Expected».
How to use the manual: (1) Start with the ”Key Points” section of each week — this
is all the ”rules” (qoidalar) of the week in a condensed form with tables; (2) Work
through the open questions (savollar) aloud, covering the answers, and check against
the model answers; (3) Complete all tests (testlar) — the same formulations are used
on exams; (4) Go through all the code line by line: on the exam, they ask ”what will
this program print?”; (5) Learn the glossary atamalar — terms appear in definition
questions; (6) Before the exam, review all bug hunts from chapter 6 and the cheat
sheet from chapter 7 (operator precedence, printf/scanf formats, ten answers in one
line).

Week 4 — the foundation of the entire course: C variables and data types, their sizes
and precision, integer and floating-point division, arithmetic, logical, bitwise opera-
tors, increment/decrement, compact assignment, ternary operator, type conversions
and operator precedence. Week’s laboratory: sphere precision (sphereprecision),
fixing leap year rule (leapyear), bridge to memory (bytes and character arrays) and
alphabetical join (alphabeticaljoin); in a separate LMS session — Circle precision and
Character processor tasks, and five-letter join — challenge. Below are all the rules,
questions, tests and terms of the week.
2.1 2.1. Key points (”all rules” of week 4)
C data types: declaration, variable names, constants
C is a fast, small, universal, platform-independent language; used for systems pro-
gramming (compilers and interpreters, operating systems, DBMS, microcontrollers).
C is static (compiled), typed, structured and imperative. ”C is quirky, flawed, and
an enormous success” — Ritchie. Data type of an object in memory determines the
set of values it can take and the operations that can be applied to it; C is a weakly
typed language: it allows implicit conversions and forced (potentially dangerous)
type casting.
The family of C types is small: numeric (int, float, double), character (char), user-
defined (struct, union). Basic laboratory table:

Slide clarifications: in C11, bool is a macro from <stdbool.h >; string is a CS50-

be declared. int main(void): int is the return type, void in parentheses means ”no
parameters”; void example(void): the first void means ”no return value”, the second
means ”no parameters”.
General declaration format: type variable-name [= value]. Lecture examples:

[Source: lecture4, slide 12]
Variable naming rules: names can contain letters, numbers, and _; must start with a
letter; cannot use keywords (for, while, etc.); names are case-sensitive — int x; and
int X; declare two different variables. Lecture pop quiz: int money$owed; — invalid
(character $); int totalcount; — valid; int score2; — valid; int 2ndscore; — invalid
(starts with a digit); int long; — invalid (keyword).
Constants — literal/fixed values. Integer: int i = 3; long l = 3; unsigned long ul =
3UL; hexadecimal int i = 0xA;; octal int i = 012;. Floating-point: float pi = 3.14159;
float pi = 3.141F; double pi = 3.1415926535897932384L;. Character: ’A’, ’\{}x41’ (hex),
’\{}0101’ (octal). String: ”hello world”; ”hello” ”world”
• same as ”hello world”. Enumerations: enum BOOL {NO, YES} →NO = 0, Y ES =
1; enum COLOR {R = 1, G, B, Y = 10} →G = 2, B = 3 — an enumerator without
an explicit value continues numbering from the previous one.
[Source: lecture4, slides 10–11; Week4, slide 2]
Sizes, ranges, and precision: sizeof, float and double
Individual sizes depend on the machine/compiler, but guaranteed: sizeof(char) <
sizeof(short) <= sizeof(int) <= sizeof(long) and sizeof(char) < sizeof(short) <=
sizeof(float) <= sizeof(double). The unsigned version has approximately twice the
range of the signed version; signed and unsigned char differ only in arithmetic ex-
pressions. For multi-byte numbers, byte order is important: big endian — most sig-
nificant bits (MSBs) at the lowest address (powerpc processors; network order); little
endian — least significant bits (LSBs) at the lowest address (all x86-compatible pro-
cessors). This is the ”NUXI problem”.

Comparison and logical operators: short circuit
Comparison operators compare two operands and yield a ”boolean” result: in C, any
non-zero value (by convention 1) is true, 0 is false. Lecture examples: 3 > 2 →1;
2.99 > 3 →0; 3 >= 3 →1; 3 < 3 →0; ’A’ < ’B’
→1; 3 == 3 →1; ’A’ == ’a’ →0; 3 != 3 →0; 2.99 != 3 →1. Traps: == (equality) is not
= (assignment); comparison == of real variables is unreliable due to finite precision.

/* evaluates to 0 */

/* evaluates to 1 */

Increment/decrement, compact assignment and ternary operator
Postfix: x + + is shorthand for x = x + 1; y = x + + is equivalent to y = x; x = x + 1; — x
is evaluated before increment (similarly for x–). Prefix: + + x; y = + + x is equivalent
to x = x + 1; y = x; — x is evaluated after increment. Compact assignment operators
for the pattern var = var (op) expr:
x += 1
/* is the same as x = x+1 */
x -= 1
/* is the same as x = x-1 */
x *= 10
/* is the same as x = x*10 */
x /= 2
/* is the same as x = x/2 */
x %= 2
/* is the same as x = x%2 */

Slide rules: AND is true only if both operands are true; OR — if at least one; XOR —

Type conversions and operator precedence
When promoted to higher precision, data is preserved — the compiler does this au-
tomatically for expressions with mixed types; rule (with exceptions): each member
of a binary expression is promoted to the precision of the highest precision operand.
Automatic conversion char →int allows comparing and ”calculating” characters:
int i;
float f;
f = i + 3.14159; /* i is promoted to float,
f = (float)i + 3.14159 */
isupper = (c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z') ? 1 : 0;
/* c and literal constants are converted to int */
if (!isupper)
c = c - 'a' + 'A';
/* subtraction is possible because of integer conversion */
Precedence and order of evaluation: ++, −−, (cast), sizeof — highest precedence; *,
/, % higher than +, −; ==, != higher than &&, ||; assignment operators — very low.
Use parentheses ( ) generously to avoid ambiguities and side effects of precedence:
y = x*3+2
/* same as y = (x*3)+2 */
x != 0 && y == 0
/* same as (x != 0) && (y == 0) */
d = c >= '0' && c <= '9'
/* same as d = (c >= '0') && (c <= '9') */
[Source: lecture4, slides 24–25]
Laboratory: leap year and character arrays
Leap year. Common year — 365 days (February has 28), leap year — 366 (February
29): the extra day keeps the calendar in agreement with the seasons. The rule is
read top to bottom: divisible by 400? →leap year; otherwise divisible by 100? →
common; otherwise divisible by 4? →leap year; otherwise common. 2000 — leap
year (divisible by 400); 1900 — common (divisible by 100 but not 400); 2024 — leap
year; 2025 — common; 2100 — common (exit check: divisible by 100 but not 400).
Compact laboratory expression:
year % 400 == 0 || (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0)
Repeatable input (”Go back to line 1” — CS50-style repetition pseudocode): read year
before the loop and again at the end of the while loop; year 0 or negative terminates
without classification; greater than 9999 — error message and stop. If you forget to
read again — positive year will never change, the loop will repeat forever. The first
rule year % 4 == 0 classifies 2024 and 2025 correctly — these two tests don’t reveal
the century bug; check 1900 and 2000.

model answers
S1. Laboratory warm-up: what types store integers, decimal values, and a
single character?
Answer. int — for integers; float or double — for decimal (real) values; char — for
a single character.
Execution starts with main; stdio.h declares printf, cs50.h —
getdouble.
S2. What does void mean in int main(void) and in void example(void)?
Answer. In int main(void) int is the return type, and void in parentheses means ”no
parameters”. In void example(void) the first void is ”no return value”, the second is
”no parameters”. A regular variable of type void cannot be declared.
S3. Why was double chosen for the radius and volume of a sphere, not float?
Answer. The radius can have a fractional part, and on our platform double is more
precise than float: 15 significant decimal digits versus 6 (DBLDIG versus FLTDIG).
At the same time, double doesn’t make the approximation pi = 3.1415 exact — real
values remain approximate.
S4. What will double fraction = 4
3; printf(”%f\{}n”, fraction); print?
Answer. 1.000000. Division occurs before assignment: both operands are integers,
4/3 gives 1, and only then is 1 converted to double. The receiver type doesn’t change
how division is performed — the operand types determine it. Similarly, (double)(4/3)
gives 1.0, while 4.0/3.0 gives 1.333333.
S5. The sphere program prints the same volume for radius = 3 with both %.1f
and %.4f. Do extra digits improve the stored value?
Answer. No. The outputs are 113.1 and 113.0940: these are the same stored number;
formatting only changes the representation (printf precision controls the display, not
the stored value).

S6. Pop quiz II from lecture: int x = 017; int y = 12; — is x greater than y?
Answer. Yes. 017 is an octal literal (like int i = 012; from the constants table — octal
number): 017₈ = 1 · 8 + 7 = 15, and 15 > 12.
S7.
What is XL in enum sz {S = 0, L = 3, XL}; and in enum sz {S = 0, L =
−3, XL};?
Answer. An enumerator without an explicit value continues numbering from the pre-
vious one — as in enum COLOR {R = 1, G, B, Y = 10}, where G = 2, B = 3. Therefore,
in the first case XL = 4, in the second XL = −2.
S8. Why does ’A’ < ’B’ give 1, while ’A’ == ’a’ gives 0?
Answer. char is automatically converted to int (the character code). The codes for
’A’ and ’B’ are in ascending order, so comparing the codes gives 1; the codes for ’A’
and ’a’ are different, so equality is false. This same conversion allows for arithmetic
like c = c - ’a’ + ’A’; (converting lowercase to uppercase).
S9. What is short-circuit evaluation and what happens to x in (0) && ((x =
x + 1) > 0)?
Answer. Expression evaluation stops if the result is already determined. The left
operand of && is 0, so the entire expression is false, and the right part — with the side
effect x = x + 1 — is not evaluated at all: x won’t change. Similarly, in (3 == 3)||((c =
getchar()) == ’y’), getchar won’t be called. In the loop i < LENGTH && first[i] ==
second[i], when i = 3, access to first[3] doesn’t occur.
S10. What’s the difference between y = x + + and y = + + x?
Answer. Postfix: y = x + +; is equivalent to y = x; x = x + 1; — x is evaluated before
increment. Prefix: y = + + x; is equivalent to x = x + 1; y = x; — x is evaluated after
increment. For decrement — similarly: y = x −−and y = −−x.
S11. How does the ternary operator work in sign = x > 0 ? 1 : −1;?
Answer. This is syntactic sugar for if (x > 0) sign = 1; else sign = −1;: the condition
is before ?, the value when true is between ? and :, when false is after :. The code
becomes shorter and clearer; the second example from the slide is isodd = x % 2 == 1
? 1 : 0;.
S12. What input should the sphere volume program reject?
Answer. Zero, negative radii, and values greater than 1000: the valid range is 0 <
radius <= 1000. Checking the positive range also rejects non-finite input.
S13. Why is 1900 a common year and 2000 a leap year? Why is 2100 com-
mon?
Answer. 2000 is divisible by 400 — leap year. 1900 is divisible by 100 but not 400 —
common year; 2100 is the same (divisible by 100 but not 400), and the rule checks
divisibility by 400 before divisibility by 100. Compact condition: year % 400 == 0||
(year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0); 2024 is leap by this, 2025 is common.
S14. Why can’t the char array first[3] = {’d’, ’o’, ’g’} be printed with %s, and
what does the order in && have to do with it?
Answer. The array has exactly three characters and no terminator ’\{}0’ — it’s not
a C-string: %s would continue reading memory beyond the array until a random
zero byte. Print exactly three characters with %c. And in the comparison loop, the
boundary check must come first: i < LENGTH && first[i] == second[i] — when i = 3,
the left part is false, && skips the right part, and no array bound violation occurs.

S4. What does else if do and what happens if multiple conditions are true?
Answer. else if adds alternative control paths. Conditions are checked in order until
the first true one; the inner statement is executed only for it. If multiple conditions
are true, only the first branch is executed. The construct is equivalent to nested if.
S5. Which if does else belong to in nested ifs and how to change this?

with the outer if, the inner if must be enclosed in curly braces: if (x % 4 == 0) { if (x

limitations?
Answer. switch tests one integer (or character) variable for equality with a set of case

efficient than long if-else ladders.

Answer. Execution ”falls through” to the next case without rechecking the value. In
the melody (Example 6.1), omitting break after case 2 caused printing C, then D for

condition is evaluated first — the body may not execute at all.
S10. What does the pair of loops from §6.2.1 print and how do they differ?

then — on the loop condition.

Pointer: address (&) and dereferencing (*)
A pointer is the address of a variable in memory; the address can be used to access
and modify the variable from anywhere — this is extremely useful for data structures
(and is notoriously confusing in code). Every
variable in memory has an address.
Variables without addresses: register variables; constants/literals/preprocessor de-
fines; expressions (if the result is not a variable). The address is taken by the operator
&; the address of a variable of type t has type t \{}*:
int n = 4;
double pi = 3.14159;
int *pn = &n;
/* address of integer n */
double *ppi = π /* address of double pi */
Dereferencing/indirection — the * operator: access to a variable by address; a deref-
erenced pointer behaves like a regular variable. Null pointer — 0 (NULL): a pointer
that doesn’t reference anything:
/* prints "pi = 3.14159\n" */
printf("pi = %g\n", *ppi);
/* pi now equals 7.14159 */
*ppi = *ppi + *pn;
Pointers can be explicitly cast to any pointer type (implicit casting to/from void * is
also possible); a dereferenced pointer has a new type regardless of the actual data;
this can cause segmentation faults and other hard-to-catch errors:
ppi = (double *)pn; /* pn originally of type (int *) */
[Source: Lecture71, slides 5, 9–11]
Memory: physical and virtual, stack and heap
Physical memory — resources where data is actually stored: cache, RAM, hard disk,
removable media; they have different capacities and access speeds; memory man-
agement is one of the main functions of the OS (it moves data during execution); in
embedded processors, memory can be extremely limited. Virtual memory
• an OS abstraction: address space available to code (on a 32-bit OS < 4GB: usu-
ally 2 GB for Windows, 3-4 GB for Linux); virtual memory is mapped to different
parts of physical memory.
Used parts of virtual memory: stack and heap. Stack (stack) — where de-
clared variables are placed; heap (heap) — where dynamic memory is placed.

Functions return no more than one value. The extended Euclidean algorithm returns
gcd(a, b), x and y (ax + by = gcd) — instead of global variables, pointers can be passed

(1) Base case — the answer without another call (n == 0).
(2) Smaller

S11. What does countdown(3) and countup(3) print and why is the output
different?
Answer. countdown(3) prints 3 2 1, countup(3) prints 1 2 3. In countdown, the print
comes before the recursive call — values appear on the way down. In countup, the
print comes after the call — it waits for the smaller call to return and executes on
the way back. Both functions visit n = 0 and stop.

second branch doesn’t remember the first. Only one call executes at any moment;
